name: Propranolol

lead: Propranolol is a long-established prescription beta blocker for blood pressure, heart rhythm, migraine prevention and tremor, used off-label to ease physical symptoms of performance anxiety such as tremor and racing heartbeat. Forum users take it for social situations, aiming to look calmer and steadier.

It blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, blunting adrenaline's effect on heart rate and tremor. A 2025 meta-analysis reported no benefit over placebo or benzodiazepines for social phobia or panic disorder, with limited evidence quality. In some threads it is also promoted for bone growth and facial structure; that claim comes from cell and animal data and has not been studied in people.

paras: People use it on prescription, often taken ahead of anxiety-provoking events for the physical symptoms. Medically it is taken on an ongoing schedule for its approved conditions.
Common effects include fatigue, slow heart rate and nausea; it can worsen asthma, is contraindicated in heart block, and abrupt stopping can worsen angina. It is prescription-only in most countries.

chain: Claimed IGF-1 and BMP-2 bone signaling
angle.text: Forum posters take propranolol to calm physical anxiety symptoms before social situations, and some promote a theory that it stimulates bone growth and improves jaw and facial structure. The anxiety use is established medically; the bone idea comes from cell and animal data.

lead: Propranolol is a prescription beta blocker, a medicine that blunts the effects of adrenaline on the heart and body. Its looks-related uses fall into three groups. For infants with a visible, fast-growing infantile hemangioma, it is an approved treatment that shrinks the lesion and can reduce lasting marks on the skin.[1][2][3] For adults, it is sometimes taken off-label to take the edge off the physical signs of nerves, such as a racing heart and shaking hands, which some people link to appearing calmer and more composed in interviews, public speaking and social settings.[4][5] And in looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for social anxiety and, in some threads, for a proposed bone-growth effect.[6]

The drug was developed by the Scottish pharmacologist James W. Black in the 1960s at ICI Pharmaceuticals, patented in 1962, approved for medical use in 1964 and first marketed as Inderal in 1965. It was the first beta blocker shown to be effective for coronary artery disease and hypertension, and Black shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for beta-blocker work.[4] It is on the World Health Organization Model List of Essential Medicines, is available as a generic, and in 2023 was the 69th most prescribed medicine in the United States, with more than 9 million prescriptions.[4]

Research on propranolol is extensive for heart disease, migraine prevention, tremor and infantile hemangioma. For anxiety disorders, meta-analyses published in 2016 and 2025 concluded that the evidence base is small and does not show a benefit over placebo or benzodiazepines for social phobia or panic disorder.[7][8] Propranolol is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia.[4][9] Coverage in 2026 described it as a rising, widely shared option for everyday nerves, with pharmacists and clinicians stressing that it is a cardiovascular drug with its own risks.[10][11]
infobox: Oral (tablet, solution, extended-release capsule); other routes exist in medical settings[4]
1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to Black for beta-blocker work[4]

paras: Infantile hemangioma is a common benign vascular growth that appears as a raised red or bluish lesion in the first weeks of life, grows for several months and then shrinks over years. It affects roughly 5 to 10 percent of births, and while most lesions need no treatment, some leave residual redness, stretched skin or altered texture, and those on the lip or nose can raise psychosocial concerns.[3] Propranolol's effect on these lesions was noticed by chance in 2008 by Léauté-Labrèze and colleagues, and a 2008 New England Journal of Medicine report described its effect on severe hemangiomas.[1][3] The US FDA approved an oral propranolol solution (Hemangeol) for proliferating infantile hemangioma requiring systemic therapy in 2014, and it is now the standard first-line systemic option, with topical timolol an alternative.[3]

For adults, propranolol is used off-label for performance and situational anxiety. People who use it describe the aim as keeping hands steady and the heart rate down so that a presentation, audition, interview or social event does not show physical nerves.[4][5][11] Wikipedia records a 1987 survey in which 27 percent of symphony and opera musicians reported using beta blockers for performances, and that actors and public speakers also use it.[4] Beta blockers are also used off-label for essential tremor and for excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis).[4]

Approved uses include hypertension, angina, atrial fibrillation, prevention of further heart attacks, migraine prevention, essential tremor, hypertrophic subaortic stenosis, pheochromocytoma and, in the Hemangeol formulation, infantile hemangioma.[4][9] In the UK, beta blockers were moved from first-line to fourth-line for hypertension in 2006, partly because they perform less well than other drug classes, especially in older adults.[4]

Propranolol has been studied or used for post-traumatic stress, specific phobias and misophonia, for aggression or agitation in some psychiatric and brain-injury settings, and for toxicity from stimulant drugs.[4][12] A systematic review compared drugs for antipsychotic-induced akathisia, and a randomized trial tested propranolol on social communication and anxiety in children and young adults with autism spectrum disorder.[13][14] A randomized trial in burn patients and a randomized trial of its potential to lengthen survival time in a disabled submarine have also been published.[15][16]

Propranolol competitively blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, so adrenaline and noradrenaline have less effect on the heart, which lowers heart rate, contractility and blood pressure.[4][9] It is lipophilic and crosses the blood-brain barrier, which underlies its central effects, and at high concentrations it also blocks sodium channels.[4]

A line of research on emotional memory showed that beta-adrenergic activation strengthens memory for emotionally arousing events, which motivated studies of propranolol in post-traumatic stress; this work has also prompted ethical debate about so-called memory dampening, which some researchers argue is overstated.[4][17]

Oral bioavailability is about 25 percent because of first-pass metabolism, plasma protein binding is about 90 percent and the half-life is about 4 hours. Metabolism is mainly through CYP1A2 and CYP2D6, and about 91 percent of an oral dose is excreted in urine. Peak effect after an oral dose occurs in about 60 to 90 minutes.[4] Fluvoxamine can raise propranolol levels about five-fold and quinidine two- to three-fold, while smoking increases clearance.[4] A 1984 trial examined its pharmacokinetics during pregnancy.[18]

Common effects include fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, constipation and a slow heart rate. It can worsen asthma, and it is contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, marked bradycardia, heart block beyond first degree, asthma or COPD, overt heart failure and severe low blood pressure.[4][9] The US label warns of exacerbated angina and, in some cases, heart attack after abrupt discontinuation, and pharmacist advice reported in the press echoes that people should not stop suddenly.[9][10]

Reviews describe propranolol-induced hypoglycemia, particularly in children, and a 2025 review in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology addressed propranolol poisoning.[19][20] In overdose it can cause bradycardia, hypotension, seizures and cardiac arrest.[4] The drug may harm a fetus, and the label summarises developmental toxicology studies in rats.[4][9] Interactions include NSAIDs blunting its blood-pressure effect and raised levels of drugs such as nifedipine and diazepam.[4]

On looksmax.org, propranolol appears in threads about social anxiety and confidence, in a minority of threads about a proposed bone-growth effect, and in threads about how to obtain it without a prescription. This article does not describe sourcing. The most detailed thread, titled as an in-depth guide, begins by describing the drug as a beta blocker commonly prescribed for blood pressure and used by many for social anxiety, then argues that research suggests it could stimulate bone growth.[6]

The thread cites a report that intravenous infusion raised plasma growth hormone in normal subjects, and cell-level findings that propranolol raised expression of IGF-1, BMP-2, Runx2 and alkaline phosphatase in bone-forming cells, mediated through the beta-2 receptor pathway; it also states that much of the evidence is preclinical.[6]

Wider media coverage in 2026 described a surge of interest in a cheap prescription pill for job interviews and family events, with one headline calling it a viral 50-cent panic pill and pharmacists warning against abrupt discontinuation.[10][11] A 2019 Hacker News discussion of a study reporting that a single dose could weaken anxiety-related memories drew hundreds of comments, showing the same interest in tech circles.[21]

Propranolol has been used in sports that depend on a steady hand, including shooting, archery, golf and snooker. At the 2008 Summer Olympics the North Korean shooter Kim Jong-su tested positive for propranolol and was stripped of his medals.[4] Musicians, actors and public speakers use it for stage fright.[4] The name Inderal echoes Alderlin, the brand of the earlier drug pronethalol, and both refer to Alderley Park, the ICI headquarters.[4]

The Beta-Blocker Heart Attack Trial, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study sponsored by the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, enrolled 3,837 people aged 30 to 69 within 5 to 21 days of a heart attack. Total mortality over an average of 24 months was 7.2 percent on propranolol and 9.8 percent on placebo, and the trial was stopped nine months early.[22] A 1999 BMJ systematic review and meta-regression examined beta blockade after myocardial infarction.[23]

A 2015 New England Journal of Medicine phase 2-3 trial randomized 460 infants aged 1 to 5 months with proliferating infantile hemangioma requiring systemic therapy to placebo or one of four propranolol regimens. Success, defined as complete or nearly complete resolution at week 24, was judged by independent blinded evaluators using standardized photographs, and a regimen was chosen after an interim analysis.[2]

A 2016 systematic review of randomized trials found eight eligible studies across panic disorder, specific phobia, social phobia and PTSD, with small samples; pooled panic-disorder trials showed no statistically significant difference between propranolol and benzodiazepines in short-term treatment, and the authors judged the evidence insufficient to support routine use for any anxiety disorder.[8] A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of beta blockers included 10 studies, five of them in meta-analyses (179 participants), and found no evidence of benefit compared with placebo or benzodiazepines for social phobia or panic disorder; the authors noted that beta-blocker prescriptions for anxiety rose substantially between 2003 and 2018 without clinical guidance.[7]

Registered trials have examined propranolol for fear of tooth extraction and for emotional-memory reactivation in post-traumatic stress, the latter terminated early with five participants.[24][25] No clinical studies of propranolol for bone growth, height or facial structure were found.

lore.intro: Forum discussion centers on propranolol as a way to quiet physical anxiety symptoms, on a proposed bone-growth effect, and on access and side effects; media coverage in 2026 describes similar public interest.[6][10][11]
